title: Culture is being recognized as development infrastructure while creative work, participation, and artistic freedom remain unevenly protected
source_unit: UNESCO, Global Report on Cultural Policies: Culture: The Missing SDG, and Re|Shaping Policies for Creativity 2026
geography: Global cultural policy, cultural and creative industries, artists and cultural professionals, digital cultural markets, and reporting Member States

denominator.unit: national and local reports submitted to UNESCO for the Global Report, more than

culture_in_development_plans.unit: percent of reporting Member States recognizing culture's importance in national sustainable-development plans

cci_in_development_plans.unit: percent of reporting countries including cultural and creative industries in national development plans

specific_cultural_objectives.unit: percent of reporting countries setting specific cultural objectives

cultural_policy_measures.unit: cultural policies and measures adopted by Parties to the 2005 Convention, more than

observations.method: UNESCO synthesis of national and local reports, policy measures, comparative cultural-policy indicators, and implementation reporting.
observations.uncertainty: Policy recognition and reported measures do not establish implementation quality, funding adequacy, participation, cultural rights, or durable social and economic outcomes.
observations.subgroup: National and local governments, cultural institutions, artists, cultural workers, communities, educators, creative firms, and cultural audiences.
observations.counterinterpretation: A broad development-plan commitment can still support meaningful cultural investment even where specific objectives or outcome indicators are not yet visible.

observations.period: 2023-2024; cultural and creative economy scale and public support

denominator.unit: global cultural and creative industries economic frame

cci_gdp_share.unit: percent of global GDP generated by cultural and creative industries, approximately

cci_jobs_share.unit: percent average share of jobs represented by cultural and creative industries

cultural_goods_trade.unit: US dollars in global trade in cultural goods in 2023, approximately

developing_country_goods_export_share.unit: percent of cultural-goods exports originating in developing countries

developing_country_services_trade_share.unit: percent of global cultural-services trade accounted for by developing countries, slightly more than

observations.method: UNESCO compilation and analysis of cultural and creative industry output, employment, and trade indicators.
observations.uncertainty: Industry boundaries, informal work, country coverage, and trade classifications vary; economic scale does not establish equitable income, cultural diversity, worker security, or audience access.
observations.subgroup: Creative firms, independent artists, cultural workers, exporters, digital distributors, developing-country producers, and audiences.
observations.counterinterpretation: Creative-industry growth and cross-border trade can expand cultural exchange, employment, and voice even where distributional and platform-power problems persist.

observations.period: 2024-2026; cultural-work protection, mobility, and artistic freedom

denominator.unit: reporting-country cultural-work and artistic-freedom policy frame

artists_rights_protection.unit: percent of artists and culture professionals reporting adequate or strong protection of economic and social rights

inward_artist_mobility.unit: percent of developed countries facilitating inward artistic mobility from developing nations

independent_artistic_freedom_monitoring.unit: percent of countries maintaining independent monitoring bodies for artistic freedom

protection_in_conflict.unit: percent of countries reporting initiatives to protect cultural professionals at risk amid instability, conflict, and displacement

cultural_public_funding.unit: percent of global GDP or less in direct public funding for culture, according to UNESCO report summary

observations.method: UNESCO comparative reporting on artist rights, mobility policy, monitoring institutions, protection initiatives, and public cultural funding.
observations.uncertainty: Reported policy mechanisms do not establish whether artists receive protection in practice, whether mobility is affordable, or whether monitoring produces remedy and safety.
observations.subgroup: Artists, cultural professionals, displaced and at-risk creators, women, developing-country cultural workers, host institutions, and public funders.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal monitoring, mobility programs, and targeted cultural funds can create meaningful protection and opportunity even when coverage remains incomplete.

observations.period: 2018-2028; digital creative work, AI, and platform distribution

denominator.unit: global digital cultural-production and distribution frame

digital_creator_income.unit: percent of creator income represented by digital revenues, up from 17 percent in 2018

music_ai_revenue_risk.unit: percent projected global revenue loss for music creators by 2028 from generative-AI outputs

audiovisual_ai_revenue_risk.unit: percent projected global revenue loss for audiovisual creators by 2028 from generative-AI outputs

digital_skills_developed_countries.unit: percent of people in developed countries holding essential digital skills

digital_skills_developing_countries.unit: percent of people in developing countries holding essential digital skills

digital_consumption_statistics.unit: percent of countries developing statistics to monitor digital cultural consumption

observations.method: UNESCO analysis of creator income, digital skills, platform distribution, copyright exposure, and modeled generative-AI effects on cultural revenues.
observations.uncertainty: Revenue projections are modeled rather than realized losses; digital income share does not identify creator-level earnings, bargaining power, ownership, or audience welfare.
observations.subgroup: Music and audiovisual creators, platform-distributed cultural workers, digital audiences, developing-country producers, rights holders, and AI firms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital tools and generative AI can lower production barriers, expand audiences, and generate new forms of creative work if rights, compensation, transparency, and access improve.

related_sources.claim: UNESCO Global Report on Cultural Policies landing page, 1,200-plus national and local report basis, chapters, and key figures.
UNESCO 2026 Re|Shaping Policies for Creativity summary covering creative trade, funding, mobility, digital revenue, AI exposure, skills, and artistic freedom.

boundary: This record adds a culture-as-development-infrastructure route linking public recognition, creative-economy scale, artist protection, digital distribution, AI exposure, cultural participation, and institutional legitimacy. It is not creator-level income, audience behavior, respondent identity, proof of policy implementation, or evidence that cultural policy automatically causes social cohesion or political action.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UNESCO Global Report on Cultural Policies page and 2026 Re|Shaping Policies for Creativity summary were reviewed; report basis, policy recognition, creative-economy scale, trade, funding, mobility, artist protection, digital income, AI exposure, skills, and monitoring claims were cross-checked.
